title: Episode 116: James Madison and the Burning of Washington: The Storm That Saved the Capital
description:
In August eighteen-fourteen, the United States was locked in the darkest days of the War of eighteen-twelve. With Napoleon Bonaparte defeated in Europe, the British Empire turned its full military might toward punishing its former colonies. A seasoned expeditionary force of four thousand British redcoats under Major General Robert Ross landed in Maryland and marched relentlessly toward Washington, D.C. At the Battle of Bladensburg, poorly trained American militia collapsed in a rout so humiliating it became known as the 'Bladensburg Races,' leaving the young capital completely undefended.

As President James Madison hurried to the front lines, his wife, First Lady Dolley Madison, remained in the President's House until the final frantic moments, refusing to flee until she had secured cabinet papers, the official silver, and the famous life-size portrait of George Washington painted by Gilbert Stuart. British troops arrived hours later, ate the hot dinner prepared for the President, and set fire to the White House, the Capitol, and the Library of Congress. Yet just as the capital seemed doomed to total destruction, nature intervened with miraculous fury: an unprecedented hurricane and violent tornado tore through the city, dousing the fires, tossing British cannons through the air, and forcing the invading army to abandon their conquest. Here is the astonishing true story of the fall and resurrection of Washington.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the crucible of the War of eighteen-twelve with our fourth President, James Madison. Madison is celebrated as the Father of the Constitution, a brilliant political philosopher who shaped the legal architecture of American liberty. Yet in the summer of eighteen-fourteen, Madison faced the ultimate nightmare of any commander-in-chief: an invading foreign army marching into the capital city, burning the symbols of the republic to ashes, and sending the federal government fleeing into the wilderness. Here is George with the extraordinary story of the Burning of Washington and the miraculous storm that saved the city.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CHESAPEAKE MENACE
In the summer of eighteen-fourteen, the young United States faced an existential threat. For two years, the War of eighteen-twelve had raged along the Canadian border and across the Atlantic, with the young American navy achieving legendary single-ship victories, but the nation's land forces struggling with disorganization and logistical failures. In April eighteen-fourteen, the global balance of power shifted catastrophically when Napoleon Bonaparte abdicated the French throne and was exiled to Elba. Great Britain, freed from its titanic two-decade struggle against imperial France, could now divert thousands of veteran soldiers and dozens of Royal Navy ships of the line to crush the American rebellion once and for all.
In August, a British armada carrying four thousand battle-hardened infantry under Major General Robert Ross and the aggressive, vengeful Rear Admiral Sir George Cockburn sailed into the Chesapeake Bay. Their mission was retributive: in eighteen-thirteen, American troops had raided and burned public buildings in York, the capital of Upper Canada, now modern-day Toronto. The British High Command was determined to inflict a humiliating retaliatory strike upon the American heartland.
Despite clear intelligence that British transports were massing in the Patuxent River just forty miles from Washington, President James Madison and his Secretary of War, John Armstrong, refused to believe the capital was the target. Armstrong stubbornly insisted that Washington was of no strategic military importance and that the British would surely strike the wealthy, fortified commercial hub of Baltimore. Consequently, virtually no defensive earthworks were dug, no permanent garrisons were stationed, and the defense of the nation's capital was left to a disorganized patchwork of raw, untrained militia.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DEBACLE AT BLADENSBURG
On the sweltering morning of August twenty-fourth, eighteen-fourteen, General Ross's redcoats marched toward the small crossroads town of Bladensburg, Maryland, six miles northeast of Washington. The town held the only bridge across the Eastern Branch of the Potomac River, making it the gateway to the undefended capital. Arrayed on the heights above the river were seven thousand American troops, commanded by Brigadier General William Winder. On paper, the Americans held superior numbers and high ground, but the troops were exhausted from days of marching in ninety-degree heat, and few had ever stood in the face of disciplined British infantry.
President James Madison, dressed in black broadcloth and carrying dual dueling pistols in his holsters, rode out to the battlefield alongside his Secretary of State, James Monroe. It remains the only time in American history that a sitting President has come under direct enemy fire on the field of battle. Madison quickly realized that the American defensive lines were a chaotic mess. The militia units were stationed too far apart to support one another, and artillery batteries had no clear fields of fire.
When the British vanguard reached the bridge, they unleashed a terrifying barrage of Congreve rockets—screaming, fiery projectiles that left trails of thick black smoke and exploded with deafening roars. The psychological effect on the untested militia was instantaneous. Men dropped their muskets and fled in absolute panic. Only a contingent of four hundred United States Marines and seasoned naval flotillamen under Commodore Joshua Barney stood their ground, engaging in ferocious hand-to-hand combat until they were overwhelmed on their flanks. As the American army disintegrated into a frantic stampede toward Maryland and Virginia, the battle was mockingly dubbed the 'Bladensburg Races.' The road to Washington lay wide open.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: DOLLEY MADISON'S DEFIANCE
While the battle raged at Bladensburg, Washington was paralyzed by panic. Government clerks packed state records into coarse linen sacks and loaded them onto wagons, while citizens fled into the Maryland hills. At the President's House, First Lady Dolley Madison waited anxiously for word from her husband. A woman of immense poise, charm, and intelligence, Dolley was widely beloved across Washington society, having single-handedly forged a culture of bipartisan hospitality in the raw new capital city.
As the distant thunder of cannon and rocket fire echoed across the Potomac, friends begged Dolley to flee immediately. The British were advancing rapidly, and rumors circulated that Admiral Cockburn intended to capture the President's wife and parade her through the streets of London as a trophy of war. Dolley refused to move. She ordered wagons brought to the portico and began supervising the evacuation of irreplaceable national treasures, including the original draft of the Declaration of Independence, the official cabinet papers, and the presidential silver.
Standing on the roof with a spyglass, she watched the dusty roads for the President's messenger. Around three in the afternoon, a courier galloped up to the house shouting, 'Fly, Madam, fly! The army is defeated and the British are within two hours of the city!' Still, Dolley refused to abandon one final, treasured relic: the massive, eight-foot-tall life-size portrait of George Washington, painted in seventeen-ninety-six by Gilbert Stuart, which hung bolted to the wall of the state dining room.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: SAVING THE FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY
The portrait of Washington was not merely a piece of art; it was the secular icon of the American republic, the living embodiment of the nation's founding virtues. Dolley knew that if British troops captured the portrait, it would be desecrated or shipped to England as an object of imperial ridicule. She ordered the household servants and a French doorkeeper named John Sioussat to unbolt the heavy gilded frame from the wall. But the screws were rusted tight, and the massive frame could not be moved with ordinary tools.
With British bayonets drawing closer by the minute, Dolley ordered the frame smashed to pieces with an ax. An enslaved personal servant named Paul Jennings, just fifteen years old at the time, worked frantically alongside the white staff to break the heavy molding and carefully slice the canvas from its stretcher bars. Dolley rolled the precious canvas, entrusted it to two gentlemen from New York who promised to transport it safely into the Maryland countryside, and only then stepped into her carriage.
Years later, Paul Jennings wrote the first White House memoir, providing an eyewitness account of that terrifying afternoon. He noted that while popular legend portrayed Dolley cutting the canvas with a kitchen carving knife, it was in fact the collaborative labor of the household staff acting under her unwavering command that preserved the masterpiece. Thanks to Dolley Madison's courage, the Lansdowne portrait survived unscathed, and hangs proudly in the White House today as the only item to have resided in the mansion continuously since its construction.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: WASHINGTON IN ASHES
At eight o'clock in the evening on August twenty-fourth, General Ross and Admiral Cockburn marched three companies of redcoats into the darkened, deserted streets of Washington. As they approached the unfinished United States Capitol building, snipers in a nearby home opened fire, killing General Ross's horse. In retaliation, the British blew the house apart with rockets and turned their fury upon the Capitol.
Finding the thick stone walls resistant to ordinary torches, British soldiers gathered mahogany desks, leather-bound chairs, and wooden flooring from the Supreme Court, the Senate chamber, and the House of Representatives, stacking them into massive bonfires. They piled thousands of rare books from the Library of Congress onto the flames and poured gunpowder into the pyres. Soon, intense heat shattered the marble columns, transformed the glass skylights into molten rain, and gutted the Capitol's interior.
Cockburn and Ross then marched down Pennsylvania Avenue to the President's House. Finding the dining room table set with exquisite crystal, fine wine, and a hot forty-place dinner prepared for the President and his generals, the famished British officers sat down, ate the meal, and toasted mockingly to 'Jemmy's health.' Afterward, soldiers smashed the furniture, gathered kindling, and ignited fifty torches simultaneously through the mansion's windows. By midnight, the White House, the Treasury building, the War Office, and the Washington Navy Yard were engulfed in a roaring wall of fire that illuminated the night sky for forty miles around. President Madison, watching the horizon burn from the Virginia shore of the Potomac, witnessed the deepest humiliation ever visited upon an American presidency.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE HURRICANE AND THE MIRACLE TORNADO
On the morning of August twenty-fifth, the British resumed their systematic destruction, preparing to burn the remaining government offices and the patent building. Admiral Cockburn personally led a troop to the office of the National Intelligencer, an anti-British newspaper, ordering his men to smash the presses and specifically destroy every piece of letter 'C' type so the editors could no longer print derogatory remarks about his name.
Around midday, the sky turned unnaturally dark, shifting from a bruised copper to an ominous, inky black. The oppressive ninety-degree heat gave way to a violent, howling gale. What followed was one of the most freakish meteorological events in North American history: a severe hurricane swept up the Chesapeake, spawning an extraordinary, violent tornado that tore directly down Pennsylvania Avenue.
The tornado struck the city with catastrophic fury. Roofs were torn clean off buildings, chimneys collapsed, and giant oaks were uprooted like weeds. The wind was so ferocious that it picked up heavy brass cannons and tossed them dozens of yards across the streets. Flying debris crushed British soldiers where they stood, killing at least thirty redcoats and wounding dozens more. Simultaneously, the heavens opened in a biblical deluge, dumping torrential sheets of water that instantly smothered the blazing fires across the Capitol and the White House. When a distraught Washington woman confronted Admiral Cockburn in the street, exclaiming, 'Great God, is this the way you make war?' Cockburn grimly replied, 'No, Madam, this is not war. It is the vengeance of God to drive us from your city.' Battered, demoralized, and fearing American reinforcements, General Ross ordered an immediate withdrawal under cover of night, marching his chastened army back to their ships.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PHOENIX AND THE SOVEREIGN WILL
When James and Dolley Madison returned to Washington three days later, they found a blackened, smoking ruin. The outer sandstone walls of the President's House still stood, but the interior was entirely gutted, its charred facade stained with soot. Many in Congress advocated abandoning Washington entirely, suggesting that the capital be moved permanently to Philadelphia or Lancaster. But James Madison refused to give the British a symbolic victory. He insisted that the government remain in Washington and ordered the immediate reconstruction of the public buildings.
The charred exterior sandstone of the executive mansion was whitewashed and painted white to conceal the scorch marks of the British torches, cementing its timeless popular name: The White House. Just three weeks later, the British attempted to capture Baltimore, but were repulsed at Fort McHenry, inspiring Francis Scott Key to write the Star-Spangled Banner. And four months after that, Andrew Jackson shattered the British army at the Battle of New Orleans, bringing the War of eighteen-twelve to a triumphant, patriotic conclusion.
The burning of Washington was a baptism by fire for the young republic. It proved that the American system of government did not depend on magnificent palaces or marble monuments. The buildings could be burned to ash, but the sovereign spirit of the Constitution and the courage of its people remained invincible.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Burning of Washington was the lowest point of the War of eighteen-twelve, but it became the catalyst for a renewed American national identity. Dolley Madison's courage and the storm that repelled an empire's veterans showed that the republic was built on foundations far stronger than brick and stone. Next week, we look back to James Madison's greatest achievement: the sweltering summer of seventeen eighty-seven in Philadelphia, where behind locked doors and barred windows, he forged the United States Constitution. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
